pestifer ciuis. Nam nihilo magis quadruplatoris, quam furis, quam sicarii, aut proditoris attulit definitionem. Item uitiosum est, pro argumento sumere quod in disquisitione positum est: ut si quis, que furti arguat, dicat eum esse hominem improbum, auarum, fraudulentum: ei rei testimonio esse, quod sibi furtum fecerit. Item uitiosum est, controuersiam controuersia dissoluere, hoc modo: Non conuenit Censores istum uobis satisfacere, ex eo quod ait se non potuisse adesse, ita ut iuratus fuerat: quod si ad exercitum non uenisset, idne Tribuno militum diceret? Hoc ideo uitiosum est, quia non expedita, aut iudicata res, sed impedita, et in simili controuersia posita exempli loco profertur. Item uitiosum est, cum id, de quo summa controuersia est, parum expeditur, et, quasi transactum sit, relinquitur, hoc modo:
Aperte fatur dictio, si intelligas:
Tali dari arma, qualis qui gessit fuit,
Iubet, potiri si studeamus Pergamo:
Quae ego profiteor esse mea. nam me aequum est frui
Fraternis armis, mihi que adiudicarier,
Vel quod propinquus, uel quod uirtute aemulus.

Item uitiosum est, ipsum sibi in sua oratione dissentire, et contra ea, quae ante dixerit, dicere, hoc modo:
Qua causa accusem hunc, nequeo exputando euoluere.
Nam si ueretur, quid eum accusem, qui est probus?
Sin inuerecundum animi ingenium possidet,
Quid eum accusem, qui id parui auditu existimet?
Non incommoda ratione uidetur sibi ostendisse, quare non accusaret. Quid, quod postea ait?

a pestilential citizen. For he has offered a definition no more of the prosecutor of the quadruple penalty than of a thief, a murderer, or a traitor. It is also faulty to assume as an argument that which is the subject of the investigation: as if someone, arguing a case of theft, says he is a wicked, greedy, and fraudulent man: that his having stolen from him is proof of that fact. It is also faulty to dissolve a controversy with a controversy, in this way: "It is not appropriate for the Censors to satisfy you regarding this matter, on the grounds that he says he could not be present as he had sworn: for if he had not come to the army, would he say this to the Military Tribune?" This is faulty because the matter is not settled or adjudicated, but rather hindered and placed in a similar controversy used as an example. It is also faulty when that about which the main controversy exists is barely explained, and it is left as if it had been resolved, in this way:
The statement speaks openly, if you understand:
He orders arms to be given to one such as the one who wore them was,
If we are eager to master Pergamum:
Which I profess to be my own. For it is right that I enjoy
My brother's arms, and that they be adjudicated to me,
Whether because I am a kinsman, or because I am a rival in virtue.

It is also faulty for the speaker to dissent from himself in his own speech, and to say the opposite of what he had said before, in this way:
What reason I should accuse him for, I cannot unravel by searching.
For if he is feared, why accuse him, who is upright?
But if he possesses a shameless disposition of mind,
Why accuse him, who considers that of little account in hearing?
He seems to have shown in no inconvenient way why he should not accuse. What, then, does he say afterward?

Comment purifiera-t-on le lieu (où ces personnes seront mortes) ? Comment ce lieu sera-t-il pur ?

Ormusd répondit : on lavera trois fois la place que le corps (aura occupée) ; on lavera trois fois les vêtemens (qui seront dans ce lieu) ; on récitera trois fois la parole ; on fera izefchné au feu ; on liera le Barsom ; on portera l'eau pure, le Zour. Après cela ce lieu sera pur : l'eau peut y couler, les arbres peuvent y croître, les Amschaspands peuvent y aller, ô Sapetman Zoroastre.

Si un petit-fils vient à mourir, ou (si) une petite fille vient à mourir, combien leurs (parens) feront-ils de prieres à Dahman, le grand-pere pour son petit-fils, la grand'mere pour sa petite-fille ? Combien (cette action leur remettra-t-elle) de Tanafours ?

Ormusd répondit : (ils feront) vingt-cinq prieres à Dahman ; (ce qui répond à) cinquante Tanafours.

### DE MOTIONE & COMPARA-
### tione Adjectivorum.

52. Adjectiva Generis omnis sunt. 1. in αρ & αξ: ὁ, ἡ, τὸ μάκαρ beatus: ἅρπαξ rapax. Sed Neutra rara. Ab αρ est Fam. Ion. & Poet. μάκαιρα, μακάρειρα.
translation:
47. Oblique cases formed by <term>syncope</term> <gloss>contraction by omitting a letter</gloss> belong here, such as ἀνδρὸς <gloss>of a man</gloss>, from ἀνὴρ <gloss>man</gloss> (c. 27), and γυναικὸς <gloss>of a woman</gloss>, θυγατρὸς <gloss>of a daughter</gloss>, etc. Likewise μία <gloss>one</gloss>, μιᾶς, with its compounds.

48. Participles are excepted, such as θείς <gloss>he who placed</gloss>, θέντος. Also πάντων <gloss>of all</gloss>, πᾶσι <gloss>to all</gloss>, δμώων, παίδων, τρώων, δᾴδων, φώτων, κράτων, φώδων. (δμὼς <gloss>servant</gloss>, παῖς <gloss>child</gloss>, τρὼς <gloss>Trojan</gloss>, δᾴς <gloss>torch</gloss>, θὼς <gloss>jackal</gloss>. κρὰς <gloss>head</gloss>; ὁ φὼς <gloss>man</gloss>; ἡ φὼς <gloss>the junction at the legs</gloss>.)

49. Τίς <gloss>who? (interrogative)</gloss> is always paroxytone; τις <gloss>someone (indefinite)</gloss> is oxytone (when it carries an accent, see c. 190).

50. The Vocative in ερ from ηρ draws back the accent (c. 16, 18. W. 86. V I). Thus γύναι <gloss>O woman</gloss>, from γυνὴ (in reality from γύναιξ, c. 33).

51. Paroxytone adjectives in ης and ων, as well as proper names in ης of the Third Declension, become proparoxytone in the Vocative: αὔταρκης <gloss>self-sufficient</gloss>, αὔταρκες; ὁ Σωκράτης <gloss>Socrates</gloss>, ὦ Σώκρατες; ὁ εὐδαίμων <gloss>happy</gloss>, ὦ εὔδαιμον.

### Regarding the Motion and Comparison of Adjectives.

52. Adjectives of all genders exist. 1. In αρ and αξ: ὁ, ἡ, τὸ μάκαρ <gloss>blessed</gloss>; ἅρπαξ <gloss>rapacious</gloss>. But neuters are rare. From αρ comes the feminine Ion. and poet. μάκαιρα, μακάρειρα.

## Rittershusius, a most wise man,

Your affection for me, most wise Rittershusius, is noble and provides me with the greatest pleasure. Your orderly character and your noble pursuit of the fine disciplines are also evident to me from the letter you wrote to our mutual friend, the most learned Eschelius, addressing my Anacreontic hymns. As the saying goes, I recognized the lion from its claws. I know well that I shall be stirred to reciprocate your kindness—not in a petty or stingy manner, but with as much sincere love as I can muster—if only you continue to be the source of such inspiration for me, and for those who issue commands from abroad. De ce que tu me demandes cóseil, certes mon conseil est tel, que ie le puis plus aisemét prendre pour moy, que d'en donner à autruy. Car y a-il choses, que i'osasse suader à toy, homme de si grande authorité & prudence?

Si nous cerchons ce qui est droit & iuste, cela est tout clair: si nous consultons du moyen le plus seur, & le plus expedient, cela est obscur & douteux: mais si nous sómes tels q deuós estre, de maniere que ne pésions rien estre vtile, qui ne soit iuste & honneste, nous ne pouuons douter de ce qu'il nous faut faire.

for although he had a mandate from you (as you write) to communicate all things to me by word of mouth, he did not come to me, and sent your letters to me by another; and I understood them to be brief, because you thought that he himself would bring them to me.

Nevertheless, after I read them, your wife Posthumia and your son Servius spoke with me. Their advice was that you should come to the Cuman villa, and they have urged me to write this to you.

As for your asking for my counsel, certainly my counsel is such that I can more easily take it for myself than give it to another. For is there anything I would dare to suggest to you, a man of such great authority and prudence?

If we seek what is right and just, that is quite clear: if we consult the safest and most expedient means, that is obscure and doubtful: but if we are as we ought to be, such that we consider nothing to be useful that is not just and honest, we cannot doubt what we must do.

Sorori (5), quam coheredem fratribus quatuor in bonis matris esse placuit, quinta portio, pro portionibus, quæ ad eos pertinuit, cedet (6) : ita ut singuli in quarta, quam antehac habere credebantur, non amplius ei quintam conferant.
§. 1. Sumptus, qui propter onera totius hereditatis justi fiunt, ei, qui patroni (7) jure portionem (8) evicerit, pro rata computentur.

7. JULIANUS lib. 8. Digestorum.
Non (9) possumus consequi per hereditatis petitionem id, quod familiæ herciscundæ judicio consequimur, ut a communione discedamus (10) : cum ad officium Judicis (11) nihil amplius pertineat, quam ut partem (12) hereditatis pro indiviso restitui mihi jubeat.

*Si possessor partem defendat, pro parte cedat.*

8. IDEM lib. 48. Digestorum.
Permittendum erit possessori hereditatis, partem (13) quidem hereditatis defendere (14), parte vero cedere. Nec enim prohibet, aliquem totam hereditatem possidere, et partem scire dimidiam ad se pertinere, de altera parte controversiam non facere.

*De procuratore, et herede heredis ante testatorem defuncti.*

9. PAULUS lib. 3. Epitomarum Alfeni Digestorum.
Cum multi heredes instituti essent, ex his unus in Asia erat, ejus procurator venditionem fecit, et pecuniam pro parte ejus abstulerat : postea apparuerit, cum, qui in Asia erat, antea decessisse, instituto ex parte dimidia herede procuratore suo, et ex parte, alio : Quæsitum est, quemadmodum pecunia ex hereditate petenda esset? Responsum est, ab eo, qui procurator (15) ejus fuisset, totam hereditatem, quia ex hereditate ea pecunia fuisset, quæ ad procuratorem ex venditione pervenisset, petere eos oportere : et nihilominus partem dimidiam hereditatis a coheredibus ejus. ita fore, sive omnis ea pecunia penes eum, qui procurator fuisset, resideret, ut omnem per Judicem ab eodem recuperarent : sive is partem dimidiam coheredi suo reddidisset, ipsum ex dimidia parte, [et] ex dimidia coheredes ejus condemnarent.

<column-break/>

*De eo, qui negotia hereditaria nomine absentis gessit.*

10. PAPINIANUS lib. 6. Quæstionum.
Cum heredis ex parte instituti filius, qui patrem suum ignorabat vivo testatore decessisse, partem hereditatis, nomine patris, [ut] absentis , administraverit (16), et pecunias, distractis rebus, acceperit, hereditas ab eo peti non potest (17) : quia neque (18) pro herede, neque pro possessore pretia possidet, sed ut filius patris negotium curavit : Negotiorum autem gestorum actio cæteris coheredibus, ad quos portio defuncti pertinet, dabitur. Illud [enim] utique non est metuendum, ne etiam patris (a quo forte exheredatus est) teneatur heredibus, quasi negotia hereditaria gesserit : cum id, quod administravit, non fuerit paternæ hereditatis. Nam et si negotiorum gestorum actio sit ei, cujus nomine per-ceptum est : ei cujus nomine, restitui æquum est. Sed in proposito neque patris negotia fuerunt, qui esse desierat : neque paternæ successionis, quæ fuerunt alterius hereditatis. Quod si filius iste patri suo heres extitit, et movet controversiam, quod pater ejus, postquam heres extitit, mortem obierit, ille tractatus incurrit, an ipse sibi causam (19) possessionis mutare videatur? Quoniam tamen qui negotia hereditaria gessit, et debitor esse cœpit, postea faciens controversiam hereditatis, ut juris possessor, convenitur, idem etiam in hoc filio respondendum erit.

4. ULPIANUS, book 15 on the Edict.
And, if fewer are born, the remainder accrues to him <note>original: "ei"</note> in proportion: if more than three, it decreases from that share from which he was made heir.

Concerning the institution of posthumous heirs and an outsider.

5. PAULUS, book 17 on the Edict.
That must be known: if a woman is not pregnant, but is thought to be pregnant, in the meantime the son is heir to the whole, although he is ignorant that he is heir to the whole.
§ 1. The same applies to an outsider, if he has been instituted heir for a certain portion: for the remainder, posthumous children. But if by chance the institution was made thus: "Whosoever shall be born to me, and Lucius Titius, shall be my heirs for their proportional shares": it will have a hesitation, whether he who does not know his portion in the testament can enter upon the inheritance? But it is more useful that he who does not know his portion can enter, if he is not ignorant of the other things which he ought to know.

Concerning the portion to be conferred upon the petitioner. 1. Concerning expenses.

6. ULPIANUS, book 6 of Opinions.
To the sister, whom it was decided should be a co-heir to the four brothers in the mother's property, a fifth portion shall yield, for the portions that pertained to them: in such a way that each of them, in the fourth which they were previously believed to have, do not confer more than a fifth upon her.
§ 1. Expenses which are made justly on account of the burdens of the whole inheritance shall be computed in proportion for him who has recovered a portion by the right of a patron.

What we obtain by this action.

7. JULIANUS, book 8 of the Digests.
We cannot obtain through the petition for an inheritance that which we obtain by the action for the partition of an inheritance, that we may depart from the communion: since nothing more pertains to the office of the judge than that he orders the part of the inheritance to be restored to me in an undivided state.

If a possessor defends a part, he may yield for a part.

8. THE SAME, book 48 of the Digests.
It shall be permitted to the possessor of an inheritance to defend a part of the inheritance, while yielding on another part. For it does not prohibit someone from possessing the whole inheritance, and knowing that a half-share pertains to himself, while not making a controversy regarding the other part.

Concerning a procurator, and the heir of an heir who died before the testator.

9. PAULUS, book 3 of the Epitomes of Alfenus' Digests.
When many heirs had been instituted, one of them was in Asia; his procurator made a sale and had taken the money for his share: afterwards it appeared that he who was in Asia had died beforehand, with his procurator instituted as heir for a half-share, and another for the other half: It was asked, in what manner the money from the inheritance ought to be petitioned? It was answered that they ought to petition the whole inheritance from him who had been his procurator, because that money had come from the inheritance which reached the procurator from the sale: and nevertheless petition for the half-share of the inheritance from his co-heirs. Thus it will be, whether all that money resided with him who had been the procurator, so that they recovered everything from the same person through a judge: or whether he had returned the half-share to his co-heir, they would condemn him for the half-share, and his co-heirs for the half.

<column-break/>

Concerning him who managed hereditary business in the name of an absent person.

10. PAPINIANUS, book 6 of Questions.
When the son of an heir instituted for a part, who was ignorant that his father had died while the testator was alive, administered a part of the inheritance in the name of his father, as if he were absent, and received monies, having sold the things, the inheritance cannot be petitioned from him: because he possesses the prices neither as an heir nor as a possessor, but managed the business as the son of his father: However, an action for managed business <note>original: "negotiorum gestorum"</note> will be given to the other co-heirs to whom the portion of the deceased pertains. That, indeed, is certainly not to be feared, that he might also be held liable to the heirs of the father (by whom perhaps he was disinherited), as if he had managed hereditary business: since that which he administered was not part of the father's inheritance. For even if an action for managed business exists for him in whose name it was received, it is equitable that it be restored to him in whose name it was. But in the case proposed, it was neither the business of the father, who had ceased to exist, nor of the father's succession, which belonged to another inheritance. But if this son became heir to his father, and moves a controversy, because his father died after he became heir, that discussion occurs: whether he seems to change the cause of possession for himself? Since, however, he who managed hereditary business and began to be a debtor is afterwards sued when he makes a controversy about the inheritance as a possessor of right, the same must be answered regarding this son.

4 Quo fit etiam vt omnia corruptissima sequantur, & populus & respublica necessario seditionibus & gladibus agitetur. Nisi enim vnaquæque trium formarum recepta reipublicæ species, in sua natura conseruetur necessarium est, quod & facile fit, eas in vitia proxima sibi collabi: monarchia habet vitium vicinum, tyrannidem, in quam leui negotio declinat.

BOOK FIVE.

rather looks to the degeneration of administration than to a certain form. The nature of monarchy is one thing, that of aristocracy another, that of democracy another, which, if they are mixed, extinguish each other: and different laws also befit monarchical administration, others aristocratic, others democratic, because they are different modes of administration. Hence also there arises an incurable error in the republic among those who promise that they will reform everything, because they confuse these things, as if on a stage they wish to arrange all things with one boot and one rule, when yet one shoe does not fit every foot, or one foot does not have every shoe that fits it.

4 From this it also follows that all most corrupt things follow, and the people and the republic are necessarily agitated by seditions and swords. Unless each of the three received species of a republic is preserved in its own nature, it is necessary—and it happens easily—that they collapse into their neighboring vices: monarchy has a neighboring vice, tyranny, into which it declines with little effort.

The government of the best men, or aristocracy, easily declines also into an allied vice, namely the power of the few, with the other best men expelled, just as democracy, or the authority of the whole people, declines into plebeian madness and lawless liberty. See Aristotle in the third book of the *Politics*, chapter five, and the fourth book, chapter two.

<margin>a In the epitome of his book 6.</margin> It has been observed by Polybius, most excellently, that just as rust to iron and worms or wood-borers to wood, when they mix, bring ruin, so that even if they escape all external harms, they are consumed by those things which are innate to them: in this way also to republics, for every one according to its nature, a certain peculiar malice grows and adheres. As for example a kingdom, which is monarchy among the willing, becomes tyranny; aristocracy becomes oligarchy; democracy becomes bestial, a *chaerocracy* <gloss>mob-rule</gloss> or sedition of the plebeians.

<margin>b Diogenes Laertius in the life of Plato, book 3.</margin> Plato, distributing the city or polity into five species, has encompassed the legitimate and the illegitimate or deficient republics. He says there are popular, aristocratic, oligarchic, royal, and tyrannical republics. Popular, in those cities in which the matter is acted upon according to the command of the multitude and magistrates are chosen by its nod, and laws are passed according to its judgment.

Aristocracy, or the rule of the best, where neither the rich nor the poor, nor those illustrious by nobility or glory, dominate, but those alone who are the best in the city administer the matter.

Oligarchy, when magistrates are chosen by property qualifications, for they are fewer than the poor.

5 He says a kingdom is twofold: one according to law, another according to lineage. He says the kingdom of the Carthaginians consists according to law, since it is civil; but that of the Lacedaemonians according to lineage, for they have a certain succession through lineage; but it is called a tyranny when citizens, impelled and forced by violence, are ruled by someone.

<meta>continues from previous page: with the talent that he enjoyed</meta> very sharp, he abused his position to behave in an immoderately critical and reckless manner, and attributed many poems, some of which were quite charming, to younger and incompetent authors. Therefore, his audacity was chastised by Dorvillius in his <term>Vannus critica</term> <gloss>Critical Winnowing-basket/Sieve</gloss>, Amsterdam 1737, 8vo. This edition was published at Utrecht in 1732, 4to, for in the edition of the previous century, 1753, only the title page of the book was changed. But anyone who has the work of Fischer alone will easily dispense with these editions. He published the poems of Anacreon for the third time in Leipzig, 1793, 8vo, with the annotations of Baxter, Estienne, Faber, and his own, which are very rich in both critical and grammatical content, as well as a most comprehensive variety of readings. See the note on the reading of the Spaletti edition at number 21. Although the very learned old man repeated the poor revision of Baxter, he nevertheless performed a great service for Greek letters through this work of his. For he first added to this third edition the preface of the second edition, in which he discourses most diligently and with no small subtlety of mind on the value of various editions and on those matters which pertain to the literary study of these poems, and inquires whether these poems are rightly attributed to Anacreon. Furthermore, he increased the number of fragments and added epigrams of Greek poets on Anacreon. Compare the preface of Mehlhorn, page VI. The revision of Brunck is entirely new; using the Palatine manuscript <note>original: "Codex Palatinus"</note> copied by Spaletti, and the conjectures of Salmasius, Lennep, and others, he presented a more corrected Anacreon, but also indulging too much in his own wit, he emended many things in passing without providing any reasons.
